concept.name: Rights offering
concept.definition: An issue giving existing shareholders the right - but not the obligation - to buy additional shares pro rata to their holdings at a discount to the market price within a set window, usually 16 to 30 days. The rights are often transferable and tradable like ordinary shares until they expire.
concept.intuition: It is a loyalty-preserving capital raise: current owners get first claim on new shares cheaply, and those who do not want in can sell the right itself.
concept.mechanics: The company distributes rights in proportion to holdings; holders may exercise at the subscription price, sell the rights if renounceable, or let them lapse. In an insured or standby offering an investment bank backstops unexercised rights to guarantee the capital target; direct offerings have no backstop.
concept.formula: Theoretical ex-rights price = (Old shares x Price + New shares x Subscription price) / Total shares after issue.
concept.failure_modes: Dilution falls on anyone who neither exercises nor sells the rights; offerings often signal distress because the firm could not raise money conventionally, and thin rights trading makes their price erratic.
concept.misconceptions: The discount is not free money: the share price adjusts down when the stock goes ex-rights to reflect the dilution, so exercising is roughly economically neutral before weighing what the capital raise signals.
concept.example: A holder of 100 shares receives rights to buy 10 new shares at $8 versus a $10 market price; exercising costs $80, and the theoretical ex-rights price drops to about $9.82.

citations.source: Investopedia, What Is a Rights Offering (Issue)?
citations.section: Understanding the Mechanics of a Rights Offering
